  "text": "The first time Nora borrowed the library’s sewing machine, she carried it home in a shopping trolley.

“Bring it back Friday,” the librarian said. “And don’t worry about the buttonhole setting. Nobody understands it.”

Nora had three pairs of her husband’s trousers to shorten. Since his operation, the hems caught beneath his heels.

On Thursday evening, the needle broke.

She returned the machine with the broken pieces in an envelope and twenty pounds folded around them.

The librarian pushed the money back.

“They do that sometimes.”

“I was only sewing cotton.”

“It’s still allowed to break.”

The next week, a packet of needles had been taped inside the case. Beside it was a handwritten note: Flat side facing away from you.

By spring, Nora had repaired a curtain, replaced two zips, and made a cushion her husband said was too good to sit on. He sat on it every afternoon.

Then she stopped borrowing the machine.

In August, the librarian saw her at the returns desk, holding a gardening book she had not opened.

“How are the trousers?” he asked.

She looked down at the book.

“Oh,” he said.

A trolley rattled past them. Somewhere upstairs, a child was being persuaded to whisper.

“We’ve got some torn story-hour cushions,” he said eventually. “If you ever felt like looking.”

Nora rubbed a loose corner of the book’s plastic cover.

“I wouldn’t promise anything.”

“Of course.”

She returned on Tuesday with her scissors.

The cushions were waiting on a table by the window. There were six, all shaped like animals.

“This one’s lost an ear,” the librarian said.

“Then we’ll start there.”"
